sections.title: The three pillars & how to measure

items.q: How do metrics, logs, and traces differ, and when should each be used?
items.a:
The three pillars answer three different questions. Collapsing them into one answer usually signals a lack of production experience.
MetricsLogsTraces
Answersis something broken?what happened?where is it slow or failing?
Formnumbers aggregated over timediscrete, contextual eventsa tree of spans for one request
Costlow, roughly constant with traffichigh, grows linearlymoderate, thanks to sampling
Retentionyearsdays to weeksa few days
Best fordashboards, alerts, SLOsdetailed investigation and auditlocating bottlenecks across a service chain
The [[g:standard investigation flow]] is: a metric triggers an alert (p99 spikes) → a trace identifies the slow span → that span's logs explain why. :::deep - a [[r:common mistake]] is deriving metrics from logs, such as counting error lines to alert. It is expensive, slow, and breaks when logs are rate-limited. The code should emit counters and histograms directly. - a metric is a [[o:lossy aggregation]]: it cannot identify one specific request. That is the trace's job. - an [[g:exemplar]] in Prometheus and OTel attaches a trace ID to a histogram observation, allowing an operator to jump directly from a p99 spike on a dashboard to the trace that caused it. Mentioning this is a strong interview signal. - an emerging fourth pillar is [[o:continuous profiling]] with tools such as Pyroscope or Parca. It answers 'which line of code consumes CPU?', something a trace cannot reveal (21-linux-production-debug.jvm-network-deep-dive-on-prod.q3) - all three pillars should share the same labels (`service`, `env`, `version`) so operators can navigate between them In an OTA, flight-search p99 spikes → a trace shows that the GDS call consumes 90% of the request → the logs for that span reveal three retries after timeouts. Without a trace, the backend and integration teams can spend hours blaming each other. :::

items.q: How does OpenTelemetry propagate trace context across services and through message queues?
items.a:
A trace is a causally related set of spans. Over synchronous HTTP/RPC, W3C Trace Context commonly carries the active context and the server span becomes a child of the client span. 
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             ^  ^                                ^                ^
             |  trace-id                         parent span-id   flags
             version
Messaging is not just delayed HTTP. The producer injects context into message properties/headers using the configured propagator; instrumentation extracts it and models broker operations such as send, receive, process, and settle according to the current OpenTelemetry messaging semantic conventions. 
propagator.inject(Context.current(), record.headers(),
    (headers, key, value) -> headers.add(key, value.getBytes(UTF_8)));
:::warn Links versus parent–child Current messaging conventions use a [[g:span link]] to the message creation context by default, which represents asynchronous causality without forcing one long parent tree. For processing exactly one message, parent–child may be used when there is no conflicting ambient context and the instrumentation follows the convention's conditions. Batch processing should link each message context; choosing one message as the parent misrepresents the rest. ::: :::deep Propagation is a contract: standardize propagators, header size, trust boundaries, retries/redelivery, and what happens when headers are absent or malformed. Do not allow an untrusted external trace header to overwrite security identity; tracing context is correlation, not authentication. Head sampling decides early and is operationally cheap; tail sampling decides after collectors see enough spans and can retain policy-selected slow/error traces, but costs buffering and requires all relevant spans to reach the decision point. Tail sampling cannot recover spans already dropped by an upstream head sampler. Choose rates from traffic, investigation value, privacy, and cost—“keep 100% of every slow/error trace” is not universally affordable or even well-defined. Context can be lost at executors, callbacks, reactive boundaries, custom clients, and message libraries; virtual threads do not remove that need. Test one trace across each real boundary. Put `trace_id` in structured logs, keep baggage small and allowlisted, and never propagate PII/secrets merely for convenience (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). :::

items.q: How do RED and USE guide metric selection for services and resources?
items.a:
The two formulas complement each other. Applying each in the right place prevents the anti-pattern of measuring everything without knowing what to inspect.

[[g:RED]] — for **services** that handle requests:
- [[b:R]]ate — requests per second
- [[b:E]]rrors — failed requests per second and error ratio
- [[b:D]]uration — the distribution of processing time, using a histogram rather than an average

[[g:USE]] — for **resources** such as CPU, disks, pools, and queues:
- [[b:U]]tilization — percentage of time busy
- [[b:S]]aturation — queued demand, such as run queue, pool wait, or lag
- [[b:E]]rrors — failures in the resource itself

A minimum service dashboard has RED for critical endpoints plus USE for the connection pool, thread pool, and consumer lag.

:::tip A useful closing line
*'High utilization is not necessarily painful; [[o:saturation]] is what the customer experiences.'* A CPU at 90% with an empty run queue is healthy—it is using the capacity you paid for.
:::

:::deep
- [[r:do not measure averages]]. An average of 200 ms may combine 95% of requests at 50 ms with 5% at 3 s. Use histograms and inspect p50/p95/p99.
- [[r:do not average percentiles]] across instances. Adding the p99 of ten pods and dividing by ten produces a meaningless number. Aggregate histogram buckets first, then calculate the percentile (`histogram_quantile` over `rate(..._bucket[5m])` performs that aggregation).
- measure latency [[o:separately for successes and errors]]: failed requests often fail fast and pull p99 down, hiding the real problem
- coordinated omission occurs when server-side measurement misses time spent waiting outside its queue; add client-side or load-balancer measurements
- useful Java-service saturation signals include `hikaricp.connections.pending`, thread-pool queue length, GC pause time, and Kafka consumer lag. These four catch most incidents.
- Google's [[g:four golden signals]] are RED plus saturation. Being able to connect both frameworks is sufficient.
:::

items.q: Why can one bad label cause a cardinality explosion that takes down the entire metrics system?
items.a:
[[b:Cardinality]] is the number of distinct time series. Prometheus stores **one series for every label combination** and keeps all active series in RAM. 
# 1 series — safe
http_requests_total{service="booking"}
#
# 5 endpoints x 4 statuses x 3 methods = 60 series — still safe
http_requests_total{service="booking", endpoint="/bookings", status="200", method="POST"}
#
# + user_id (1 million users) = 60,000,000 series — failure
http_requests_total{service="booking", ..., user_id="u_8412773"}
[[r:Labels with unbounded values]] are almost always the cause: `user_id`, `booking_id`, `email`, `trace_id`, full URLs containing path IDs, or exception messages. **Prevention:** - label values must come from a [[g:finite, known set]] - normalise paths to `/bookings/{id}`, not `/bookings/8H2K`; [[r:this is the most common mistake]] - high-dimensional analysis by user or booking belongs in [[g:logs or traces]], not metrics - configure `sample_limit` in the scrape configuration so one broken service cannot take down all of Prometheus :::deep - a quick estimate: a metric's cardinality is the [[o:product]] of the value counts for all labels. Adding a label with ten values multiplies cardinality by ten; it does not add ten. - symptoms include steadily growing Prometheus RAM until OOM, progressively slower queries, and increasing `scrape_duration`. Diagnose with `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` and the `/api/v1/status/tsdb` endpoint. - using an exception message as a label is a subtle trap: `error="connection timeout to 10.0.3.41:5432"` makes each IP and port combination a new series. Use a classified [[g:error type]] such as `error="timeout"`. - histogram `le` buckets also multiply cardinality: a 12-bucket histogram creates 12 series plus two. Do not add a histogram to an already highly labeled metric. - continuous deployments plus a `version` label create churn because old series consume RAM until retention expires. Consider removing version from high-frequency metrics. - in systems billed by custom metric, such as Datadog or CloudWatch, a cardinality explosion may not crash the platform; it [[r:explodes the bill]], sometimes discovered a month later :::

items.q: What decisions should SLI, SLO, SLA, and an error budget drive?
items.a:
- [[b:SLI]] is a measured user-relevant outcome, such as the ratio of valid booking requests completed successfully within 300 ms.
- [[b:SLO]] is the target and measurement window for an SLI, plus its inclusion/exclusion rules.
- [[b:SLA]] is an external agreement; consequences may include service credits, termination rights, reporting, or other remedies—not necessarily a financial penalty in every contract.
- An [[b:error budget]] is the allowed bad portion. A 99.9% time-based objective over exactly 30 days corresponds to 43m12s; a request-based objective allows 0.1% of eligible requests, not 43 minutes.

Use budget and burn-rate data to govern risk: release pace, experiment exposure, maintenance, reliability work, and escalation. The response to exhausted budget is a policy agreed with product and engineering; it can include slowing risky changes, narrowing rollout, or prioritizing reliability, but an automatic company-wide “feature freeze” is not universal.

:::warn Separate availability from correctness
A 100% availability target is usually unrealistic and produces no learning budget. Some correctness invariants—no unbalanced ledger entry, no unauthorized transfer—are intentionally absolute and need transactional controls, reconciliation, and audit rather than being diluted into an availability SLO.
:::

:::deep
Measure at multiple meaningful points: client/edge for user experience and service boundaries for diagnosis. Define eligible events, “good,” planned maintenance, retries, partial responses, low traffic, and data latency so teams cannot reinterpret the SLO during an incident.

Request-based SLIs suit event volume; time-window SLIs can be useful for sparse traffic but hide burst size. Segment journeys with materially different expectations instead of averaging critical checkout with history browsing.

Dependency SLO multiplication is only a rough model under serial, independent, no-mitigation assumptions. Redundancy, caching, hedging, fallbacks, correlated failures, and traffic split change end-to-end availability. Measure the composed user journey and use dependency models for design, not as a mathematical ceiling.
:::

items.q: How should alerts be designed to avoid fatigue: should they fire on symptoms or causes?
items.a:
Page on a condition that is urgent, actionable, and important. User-visible symptoms and fast error-budget burn are strong defaults because they aggregate many causes. Cause-based signals can still justify a page when they predict imminent impact and require immediate action—for example exhausted queue capacity, a certificate about to expire, data-loss risk, or a failed redundancy layer before the last copy fails.
RouteContractExample
Pagea named responder must act now to limit material impactfast multi-window SLO burn, ledger invariant breach
Ticket/work queueaction has an owner and due window but can wait for business hoursslow budget burn, capacity forecast
Dashboard/eventcontext for diagnosis; no guaranteed actionCPU, pod restart, GC cycle
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts pair a short window for fast incidents with a longer confirmation window for sustained burn. Values such as 14.4× or 6× are examples derived from an SLO window and desired exhaustion time, not universal thresholds; calculate them for the actual objective and traffic. :::deep Every routed alert needs an owner, severity, tested notification path, evidence, and a first safe action. A runbook is especially valuable for operational pages, but a security or correctness alert may instead require a restricted incident procedure. Tune `for` duration to the failure mode. Five minutes may suppress noise but can be unacceptable for rapid data loss; use multi-window logic, hysteresis, grouping, inhibition, and deduplication based on evidence. “Two non-actionable alerts” is a review trigger, not an automatic delete if the signal reveals a missing capability. Measure pages, acknowledgment, actionable rate, duplicate volume, escalation, and missed incidents per rotation. There is no universal sustainable pages-per-week number: staffing, duration, severity, follow-up load, and recovery opportunity all matter. Also detect abnormal silence with expected-traffic or heartbeat signals, especially for low-error systems. :::

items.q: What is the incident-response process from the initial page through the postmortem?
items.a:
Incident response optimizes safe impact reduction while preserving the evidence and control needed for the incident type.

1. **Declare and scope:** record impact, affected journeys/tenants/data, severity, incident lead, and communication cadence.
2. **Stabilize:** choose the lowest-risk mitigation supported by evidence—rollback, disable a flag, shed/degrade load, fail over, revoke credentials, or isolate a component. A recent deployment is a strong clue, not proof that immediate rollback is always safe.
3. **Coordinate:** separate incident command, technical operations, communications, and subject expertise when incident size permits. Small teams may combine roles, but one person owns decisions and the timeline.
4. **Verify recovery:** check user SLIs, queues/backlogs, data integrity, security containment, and downstream health; “graphs turned green” may not mean work or data is correct.
5. **Transition:** preserve artifacts, define monitoring/reconciliation, communicate status, and hand off follow-up risk.

:::warn Availability and security can differ
For a routine availability incident, restore service before deep root-cause analysis. For suspected compromise, fraud, or data corruption, blindly restoring or destroying evidence can increase harm. Follow the security/data incident procedure, contain access, and involve legal/privacy/compliance roles where required.
:::

:::deep
The learning review should be blameless and evidence-based: timeline, contributing technical/organizational conditions, detection and decision quality, impact, what helped, what made recovery harder, and actions with owners and verification dates. “Five whys” is one prompt, not a mandatory proof of one root cause; complex incidents usually have interacting causes and failed defenses.

Track metrics only when they drive improvement. Time to detect/acknowledge/mitigate/recover, customer harm, data reconciliation, and recurrence can be useful, but a single MTTR average hides severity and encourages premature closure. Review distributions and qualitative decision points.

Corrective actions should reduce recurrence probability, blast radius, detection time, or recovery risk. Exercise rollback/failover, credential rotation, backups/restores, degraded modes, and communication through game days. Fintech/OTA recovery always includes reconciliation for stuck bookings, duplicate attempts, and ambiguous payment outcomes.
:::

items.q: How should structured logging and correlation be designed so logs are actually searchable?
items.a:
Structured logging starts with a versioned event schema, not with “turn every string into JSON.” A useful event normally includes a timestamp, severity, service/environment/version, a stable event name, outcome, and the fields needed to investigate that event. Add `trace_id` and `span_id` when a valid span is active; background jobs and bootstrap logs may legitimately have neither. 
{"ts":"2026-07-31T10:04:12Z","severity":"WARN","service":"booking",
 "version":"2026.07.31.2","event":"seat_hold_failed","outcome":"rejected",
 "trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6","seat":"12A","flight":"VN231",
 "reason":"already_held","duration_ms":42}
Use stable field names and bounded classifications such as `reason="already_held"`; keep free-form detail in a message field. Correlation IDs, tenant IDs, and business IDs should be allowlisted according to privacy and cardinality policy rather than copied into every event. :::tip Context lifecycle Install trace context at the ingress or job boundary and remove or restore only the keys that boundary owns. A scoped MDC API can make cleanup explicit: 
try (MDC.MDCCloseable ignored = MDC.putCloseable("trace_id", traceId)) {
    chain.doFilter(req, res);
}
Test propagation across the actual executor, virtual-thread, callback, reactive, and messaging boundaries. A `ThreadLocal`-backed MDC does not by itself establish cross-boundary propagation. ::: :::deep - Define severities as an operational contract. `ERROR` should represent a failed operation or condition that is actionable under the team's policy; it does not universally imply that a human must inspect every occurrence. - Sample or rate-limit noisy events using a risk- and cost-based policy. Security/audit events may require separate immutable retention; “100% failures and 1% successes” is not a universal safe ratio. Metrics should record aggregate rates even when individual logs are sampled. - Redact or avoid credentials, session/token material, payment data, and unnecessary personal data at the source. Appender-side masking is defense in depth, not permission to emit secrets first. - Log an exception where ownership and outcome are known. Multiple layers may emit different useful events, but duplicating the same stack trace at every rethrow adds cost without evidence. - Containerized applications commonly write to `stdout` for platform collection, while direct OTLP export, sidecars, or managed file agents can also be valid. Choose one delivery contract and specify buffering, backpressure, loss behavior, and retention. Trace/log correlation and sampling mechanics are covered in (20-observability-sre.the-three-pillars-how-to-measure.q2). Never treat trace context as authentication identity. :::
